rationale: The empirical frequency of seizures among individuals with FBXO11-related neurodevelopmental disorder falls consistently between 25% and 43% across published cohorts (5/20 in Gregor et al. 2018, 3/12 in Pan et al. 2024, and 43% in Goel et al. 2026). However, the hypothesis fails in two key assertions: first, this frequency is not substantially higher than initial index reports, as the initial 2018 discovery cohort by Gregor et al. already documented seizures in 25% (5/20) of cases. Second, seizures do not function as an active discriminating sign: they occur in a minority of affected individuals, are frequently mild or absent (Pan et al. 2024), show non-specific neuroimaging without clear epilepsy correlation (Goel et al. 2026), and are pervasive across many other genetic neurodevelopmental disorders (Zacher et al. 2021, Mainali et al. 2023).

evidence.text: In the initial discovery cohort defining FBXO11-related disorder across 20 individuals, seizures were reported in 5 of 20 affected individuals (25%), establishing that seizure prevalence was documented at 25% from the primary index cohort.

source.title: De novo variants in the F-box protein FBXO11 in 20 individuals with a variable neurodevelopmental disorder
source.quote: They present with mild to severe developmental delay associated with a range of features including short (4/20) or tall (2/20) stature, obesity (5/20), microcephaly (4/19) or macrocephaly (2/19), behavioral problems (17/20), seizures (5/20), cleft lip or palate or bifid uvula (3/20), and minor skeletal anomalies.

evidence.text: In an expanded cohort of 21 previously unreported individuals with heterozygous pathogenic FBXO11 variants, seizures were documented in 43% of patients, while neuroimaging findings were nonspecific and did not consistently correlate with epilepsy.

source.title: Defining FBXO11-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder: Clinical, Molecular and Facial Assessment of 21 Patients
source.quote: Microcephaly occurred in 24%, while seizures were present in 43%. Brain imaging abnormalities were nonspecific and did not consistently correlate with epilepsy.

evidence.text: Among 12 individuals from 5 Chinese families with FBXO11 variants, seizures were identified in 3 of 12 (25%), and severe seizures were explicitly not observed in most individuals.

source.title: FBXO11 variants are associated with intellectual disability and variable clinical manifestation in Chinese affected individuals
source.quote: In addition, severe seizures were not observed in most affected individuals... seizures (3/12)

evidence.text: In adults presenting with intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental disorders, epilepsy is widespread across dozens of monogenic etiologies, indicating seizures are common across the differential diagnoses and not discriminating for FBXO11.

source.title: The genetic landscape of intellectual disability and epilepsy in adults and the elderly: a systematic genetic work-up of 150 individuals
source.quote: Null variants in FBXO11 are associated with a syndromic form of intellectual disability... We investigated 150 adult/elderly individuals with NDDE

evidence.text: A clinical cohort of 24 individuals with FBXO11 variants defined the phenotypic core as mild-to-severe intellectual disability, behavioral problems, hypotonia, joint hyperlaxity, and distinct lip morphology, rather than epilepsy.

source.title: De novo variants in FBXO11 cause a syndromic form of ... - PMC
source.quote: All individuals had borderline to severe ID and behavioral problems (autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, aggression) were observed in most of them. The most relevant common facial features included a thin upper lip and a broad prominent space between the paramedian peaks of the upper lip.

conflicts: The initial index cohort (Gregor et al. 2018) already observed seizures in 25% (5/20) of cases, directly contradicting the premise that subsequent cohorts identified a 'substantially more frequent' manifestation than initial descriptions.

Seizures cannot act as an active discriminating sign because they are absent in the majority (57-75%) of FBXO11 patients and represent a frequent, non-specific finding across competing intellectual developmental disorders (such as those described in Zacher et al. 2021 and Mainali et al. 2023).

new_directions.question_text: What specific electroclinical seizure semiology or EEG patterns, if any, distinguish FBXO11-related epilepsy from other monogenic neurodevelopmental syndromes?
new_directions.rationale: While seizure occurrence alone has low discriminating power (25-43%), specific epilepsy syndromes or characteristic EEG anomalies could provide true differential diagnostic utility.

new_directions.question_text: How do quantitative facial gestalt algorithms (e.g., GestaltMatcher) perform in differentiating FBXO11 from clinically overlapping intellectual disability syndromes?
new_directions.rationale: Goel et al. 2026 demonstrated measurable intra-cohort facial similarity, suggesting facial morphology may possess substantially higher discriminatory value than intermittent neurological signs like seizures.
